title: The Electrical System — Alternator, Battery, and Electrical Failure

required_knowledge_points.title: Alternator vs. Battery — The Two-Source Electrical Architecture
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'You are cruising in IMC and notice the ammeter shows discharge. What has happened and what do you do?' The pilot who says 'the battery is dead' has the diagnosis partially right but misses the key point: the ALTERNATOR has failed — the battery is now the ONLY electrical source and has limited capacity. Knowing the typical battery backup time changes the urgency of action dramatically.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Aircraft electrical system architecture: (1) ALTERNATOR (or generator on older aircraft): engine-driven AC generator with a solid-state rectifier (AC to DC). Primary electrical source during normal operation. Maintains system voltage at approximately 13.5-14.2V and charges the battery whenever the engine is running. If the alternator fails, it no longer charges the battery — the battery becomes the sole source. (2) BATTERY: stores DC electrical power. Starting power source. Backup source during alternator failure. Limited capacity — typically 17-35 amp-hours depending on aircraft. With a 15-amp electrical load: a 17 AH battery lasts approximately 1 hour at full charge. Substantially less if battery is partially discharged before failure. Ammeter behavior: CHARGE (+): alternator is producing power exceeding the electrical load — excess charges the battery. Normal in most aircraft with engine running and radio/avionics on. DISCHARGE (−): system is drawing more power than the alternator produces — occurs during alternator failure (battery supplying all loads), or immediately after engine start when the battery is being recharged after starting. Sustained discharge indication after engine is established in cruise: ALTERNATOR FAILURE. Response: shed electrical load (reduce unnecessary equipment use), advise ATC, plan for landing before battery depletion.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Two-Source Electrical Architecture

| Component | Role | Failure Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Alternator** | Primary source — engine-driven, charges battery | Battery becomes sole source; clock is running |
| **Battery** | Starter power + backup | Limited capacity (~1 hr at 15A draw for 17AH battery) |

### Alternator (or Generator)
- **Engine-driven AC generator** with solid-state rectifier (AC → DC)
- Maintains system voltage at **~13.5–14.2V** and **charges the battery** while running
- When alternator fails: battery takes over — **no more charging**

### Ammeter Interpretation
| Indication | Meaning | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **CHARGE (+)** | Alternator producing surplus → charging battery | ✅ Normal in cruise |
| **Brief DISCHARGE** after start | Battery recharging after engine start | ✅ Normal — should resolve quickly |
| **Sustained DISCHARGE in cruise** | **Alternator has failed** | ⚠️ Begin load shedding; plan immediate landing |

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** A sustained discharge indication in cruise does **NOT** mean 'the battery is low.' It means the **alternator has failed** and the battery is now supplying all electrical loads. The battery has **finite capacity** — time is a factor.

required_knowledge_points.title: Electrical Load Management — What to Shed and What to Keep
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'The alternator has failed in IMC. Which electrical systems do you keep on?' Without thinking through the load management question in advance, pilots have run their batteries dry in IMC while trying to conserve — and turned off the communications equipment when they should have kept it and turned off the pitot heat, landing lights, and cowl flap heaters instead.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: After alternator failure — load shedding priority: KEEP ESSENTIAL, SHED NON-ESSENTIAL. Non-essential loads to shed FIRST (highest power draw, lowest safety value): (1) Landing lights (uses 1-3 amps). (2) Position/strobe lights if daytime (5-8W LED, minimal, but trim where possible). (3) Cabin heat electrical elements (if electrically powered). (4) Entertainment/ADF equipment not needed for navigation. (5) Non-critical avionics (DME, ADF if not navigating with it). Essential loads to KEEP: (1) COM radio — maintain communication with ATC (ATC may be able to vector to nearest airport, declare emergency, coordinate). (2) Transponder — squawk 7700, ATC radar tracking. (3) NAV/GPS — navigation to nearest airport. (4) Pitot heat — in IMC with icing conditions; losing pitot heat in visible moisture risks airspeed indicator failure. (5) Attitude indicator (if electrically powered — AI may be vacuum-powered in which case no electrical load). Battery conservation calculation: estimate electrical load after shedding. Estimate battery charge remaining. Calculate flight time to nearest airport. If battery time < flight time: DECLARE EMERGENCY, get on the ground immediately.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Load-Shedding Priority After Alternator Failure

**Principle: KEEP ESSENTIAL — SHED NON-ESSENTIAL**

#### Shed First (High Draw, Low Safety Value)
- ❌ Landing lights (1–3 amps)
- ❌ Strobe/position lights (if daytime)
- ❌ Electrically-powered cabin heat elements
- ❌ ADF / DME (if not currently navigating with them)
- ❌ Non-critical entertainment/avionics

#### Keep As Long As Possible (Essential)
- ✅ **COM radio** — ATC coordination, vectors to nearest airport
- ✅ **Transponder** — squawk 7700, maintain radar contact
- ✅ **Primary NAV/GPS** — navigation to alternate
- ✅ **Pitot heat** (if in visible moisture) — losing it in icing risks ASI failure
- ✅ **Attitude indicator** (only if electrically powered; vacuum AI draws no electrical load)

### Battery Time Calculation
1. Estimate remaining electrical load after shedding
2. Estimate remaining battery charge
3. Calculate time to nearest airport

> ⚠️ **If battery time < flight time to nearest airport → DECLARE EMERGENCY immediately.**

required_knowledge_points.title: In-Flight Electrical Fires — Smoke in the Cockpit Emergency
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE presents: 'You smell burning electrical insulation and see wisps of smoke from the instrument panel. What do you do — in order?' This is a memory-item emergency. The wrong answer: 'I'd try to figure out what's burning.' The correct answer: MASTER OFF, AVIONICS OFF, determine if the fire persists, ventilate, land immediately. Students who hesitate here have failed.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: In-flight electrical fire emergency (from POH/AFM memory items): (1) MASTER SWITCH: OFF. This removes all electrical power from the aircraft systems, eliminating the power source feeding the fire. (2) AVIONICS MASTER (if separate from master): OFF. Many glass-cockpit aircraft have a separate avionics master — turn it off independently. (3) ALL ELECTRICAL EQUIPMENT: OFF. (4) EVALUATE: Does the smoke stop? If yes → electrical short was the source; evaluate whether to restore specific critical circuit. If smoke continues → the fire may be in cabin materials (not electrical in origin) → open fresh air vents (but NOT overhead facing the fire). (5) VENTILATE: open windows/vents to clear smoke from cockpit. (6) LAND IMMEDIATELY: squawk 7700, declare emergency, land as soon as possible — even off-airport if necessary. Partial restoration: after smoke clears, SOME pilots restore avionics master only (comm radio) to contact ATC. Some POHs describe this — follow your aircraft-specific checklist. SMOKE IN COCKPIT without electrical source: check carbon monoxide detector. CO poisoning from a cracked exhaust manifold is odorless and can cause rapid incapacitation — exit heating system, ventilate, land immediately.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### In-Flight Electrical Fire — Memory Items (POH/AFM)
1. **MASTER SWITCH** → **OFF** (removes all power from the fault)
2. **AVIONICS MASTER** → **OFF** (if separate switch — glass-cockpit aircraft)
3. **ALL ELECTRICAL EQUIPMENT** → **OFF**
4. **EVALUATE:** Does smoke stop?
   - **YES** → Electrical short was the source. Consider selective restoration of COM radio only.
   - **NO** → Fire may be in cabin materials — open fresh-air vents (NOT directed at the fire)
5. **VENTILATE** cockpit — open windows/vents to clear smoke
6. **LAND IMMEDIATELY** — squawk 7700, declare emergency

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** The wrong answer is *'I'd try to identify the source first.'* The correct answer removes power from the fault **immediately** — investigation follows **after** the power is off.

### Circuit Breaker Protocol
- A tripped circuit breaker indicates a **fault in that circuit**
- **Do NOT reset** tripped breakers in flight unless:
  - The loss of that circuit is a **direct safety threat**
  - The POH explicitly authorizes a **single reset attempt**
- Never attempt a **second reset** — resetting into a live fault can re-start the fire

### Smoke Without Electrical Source → Check CO
- CO is **colorless and odorless** — cracked exhaust manifold can produce it
- Response: heat **OFF**, windows **OPEN**, supplemental O2 if available, **land immediately**

required_knowledge_points.title: Avionics Bus Architecture — Essential Bus, Avionics Bus, and Circuit Breakers
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'A circuit breaker pops in flight. What do you do?' The textbook answer: do not reset a circuit breaker in flight unless required for safety. The reason: circuit breakers trip because a circuit has exceeded its current limit — something is wrong with that circuit. Resetting it may allow the fault to persist and cause fire. This is one of the most commonly violated cockpit management rules.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Aircraft electrical bus architecture: (1) MAIN BUS (essential bus): directly powered by the alternator/battery master; powers critical engine instruments, emergency lighting, essential avionics. (2) AVIONICS BUS: powered through a separate avionics master switch; prevents avionics from seeing voltage spikes during engine start; protects sensitive electronics from starter motor voltage transients. (3) CIRCUIT BREAKERS: thermal fuses that trip when current exceeds the breaker rating; protects the wiring harness from fire caused by overcurrent. Do NOT reset: the standard guidance for in-flight circuit breaker operation is to NOT reset a tripped breaker. If a breaker trips, the circuit has a fault. Resetting it may re-close the fault and cause fire. Exception: if the loss of that circuit directly impairs safety (e.g., a flight-critical instrument), the pilot may attempt ONE reset per POH guidance — but must be prepared for the breaker to trip again immediately and not attempt a second reset. Annunciators: modern aircraft have electrical system warning lights (LOW VOLT, ALT FAIL). These should be understood and the correct response memorized before flight — not studied during an in-flight emergency.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Electrical Bus Architecture
| Bus | Powered By | Protects |
|---|---|---|
| **Main Bus (Essential Bus)** | Alternator/battery master | Critical engine instruments, emergency lighting, essential avionics |
| **Avionics Bus** | Separate avionics master switch | Sensitive avionics from engine-start voltage spikes |

### Avionics Master — Critical Rule
- **Master ON** → start engine → **Avionics master ON** *after* engine stabilizes
- **Never** have avionics master on during engine start — starter creates momentary voltage transients

### Circuit Breakers
- **Thermal fuse** — trips when circuit current exceeds rated limit
- Trip = **something is wrong** with that circuit

#### In-Flight Circuit Breaker Protocol
| Situation | Action |
|---|---|
| Breaker trips — non-critical system | **Do NOT reset** — leave it tripped |
| Breaker trips — safety-critical system | **ONE reset attempt** per POH guidance; if it trips again, **do not attempt a second reset** |

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** Resetting a tripped circuit breaker into a live fault can **re-start the electrical fire**. This is one of the most commonly violated cockpit management rules.

### Annunciators to Know
| Light | Meaning | Response |
|---|---|---|
| **LOW VOLT** | System voltage below normal | Check alternator; begin load shedding |
| **ALT FAIL** | Alternator has failed | Alternator failure procedure — land soon |

lesson_overview:
## The Electrical System -- Alternator Failure, Load Shedding, and Smoke in the Cockpit

The electrical system is the most failure-prone major system in light aircraft -- and probably the least understood by student pilots. Most students know the master switch is a split switch. Fewer can explain why a discharge ammeter at cruise means the alternator has failed rather than the battery. Fewer still can execute load-shedding priorities in sequence when the battery is the only power source remaining. This lesson closes all three gaps.

**The two-source architecture: alternator and battery, and what each does.** During normal engine operation, the alternator (or generator in older aircraft) is the primary electrical source. It is engine-driven and produces AC power that's rectified to DC. It maintains system voltage at approximately 13.5 to 14.2 volts, powers all electrical systems, AND simultaneously charges the battery. The battery is a stored-energy backup -- its primary job is engine starting, and its secondary job is providing power during alternator failure. A fully charged 17 amp-hour aircraft battery powering a 15-amp load will sustain the system for roughly one hour. Partial discharge or higher electrical loads shorten that window significantly. The ammeter tells you which scenario is active: a charge indication (positive deflection) means the alternator is producing surplus power. A sustained discharge indication (negative deflection) in cruise means the alternator has failed and the battery is now supplying everything -- the clock is running.

**Alternator failure in cruise: the first 30 seconds matter.** When the ammeter shows sustained discharge in cruise flight (after the initial battery recharge that follows engine start): diagnose alternator failure. Response: (1) Reduce unnecessary electrical loads immediately -- buy every minute of battery time you can. (2) Advise ATC -- they can direct you to the nearest suitable airport and give you priority handling. (3) Plan to land at the nearest airport -- not your destination. The battery has a finite timeline. The most common fatal error: continuing to the planned destination while assuming the battery will last, only to lose all electrical systems including communications and possibly nav on the approach.

**Load shedding: keep what matters, shed what doesn't.** When operating on battery-only, the priority is to eliminate high-power-draw, low-safety-value systems first. Shed first: landing lights (1-3 amps), strobe lights (unless night), non-navigating avionics (DME, ADF if unused), cabin electrical heaters. Keep as long as possible: COM radio (ATC coordination), transponder (squawk 7700, radar contact maintained), primary nav/GPS (navigation to alternate), pitot heat if in visible moisture (losing pitot heat in icing risks airspeed failure). The AI may be vacuum-powered -- in that case it draws no electrical load and needs no management. Know your aircraft's specific power architecture before departure.

**Electrical fire: the memory-level emergency.** Smoke from the instrument panel is not a 'let me investigate calmly' situation. The source of an electrical fire is the power still feeding the short circuit. The emergency is: (1) Master switch OFF. This removes power from the fault simultaneously. (2) Avionics master OFF if separate. (3) All electrical equipment OFF. (4) Evaluate whether smoke stops -- if yes, the source was electrical. Consider whether to restore critical systems selectively (comm radio first). (5) If smoke continues or intensifies -- the fire may be in cabin materials; open fresh-air vents but NOT directed at the fire source. (6) Declare emergency, land immediately. A circuit breaker that has tripped indicates a fault in that circuit. Do NOT reset it in flight unless the loss of that specific circuit is a direct safety threat AND the POH authorizes a single reset attempt. Resetting a tripped breaker into a live fault can re-start the fire.

**Bus architecture: the avionics master as a protection layer.** Most light aircraft have a split electrical bus: the main bus (essential bus) powers critical instruments and is energized whenever the master switch is on. The avionics bus is powered through a separate avionics master switch, protecting sensitive electronics from voltage spikes during engine cranking. Never have the avionics master on during engine start -- the starter motor creates momentary voltage transients that can damage avionics. The discipline: master ON, start engine, avionics master ON after engine stabilizes.

**The checkride trap:** The DPE says, 'Your ammeter has been showing a slight discharge for the last 15 minutes. What's happening and what's your plan?' The student who says 'the battery is low' has misdiagnosed -- the battery shows on a charge indicator after start, then neutralizes in cruise. Sustained DISCHARGE in cruise is an alternator failure signal. Correct answer: alternator has failed, battery is supplying all loads, I need to shed non-essential electrical equipment and land at the nearest suitable airport before the battery depletes.
